content: 1. The study titled E-learning and automated evaluation of cervical images for cancer screening was published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in 2019. It explores the use of digital learning and automated systems to assess cervical images for cancer screening purposes. The findings are detailed in volume 111, issue 9, pages 923–932, with the DOI reference 10.1093/jnci/djy225. 2. Lie AK and Kristensen G conducted research on the utility of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) E6/E7 mRNA testing as a predictive biomarker for cervical carcinoma. Their findings were published in the journal Expert Review of Molecular Diagnostics in 2008, volume 8, issue 4, pages 405–415. 3. Sorbye SW, Fismen S, Gutteberg TJ, Mortensen ES, and Skjeldestad FE performed a prospective cohort study on primary cervical cancer screening using an HPV mRNA test. Their work was published in BMJ Open in 2016, volume 6, issue 8, under the article ID e011981, with the DOI 10.1136/bmjopen-2016-011981. 4. Cuschieri K and Wentzensen N investigated the detection of HPV mRNA and p16 as biomarkers to improve the diagnosis of cervical neoplasia. Their research was published in Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention in 2008, volume 17, issue 10, pages 2536–2545, with the reference EPI-08-0306. 5. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidelines for the screening and treatment of precancerous lesions to prevent cervical cancer. These guidelines are accessible online through the WHO reproductive health publications. 6. The second edition of the WHO guideline for screening and treating cervical pre-cancer lesions for cervical cancer prevention provides updated recommendations and evidence-based practices. 7. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has published a handbook on cervical cancer screening as part of its cancer prevention series, volume 18. 8. Bouvard V, Wentzensen N, Mackie A, Berkhof J, Brotherton J, and Giorgi-Rossi P, among others, contributed to a special report on the IARC perspective on cervical cancer screening. This report was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, volume 385, pages 1908–1918, with the DOI 10.1056/NEJMsr2030640. 9. The WHO has also released a comprehensive guide to cervical cancer control, titled Comprehensive cervical cancer control: A guide to essential practice, now in its second edition. 10. WHO guidelines for the use of thermal ablation in treating cervical pre-cancer lesions are available online, providing detailed recommendations for this treatment modality. 11. A step-by-step guide for introducing and scaling up HPV testing as part of a comprehensive cervical cancer prevention and control program has been published by the WHO. 12. The WHO handbook for guideline development, now in its second edition, outlines the processes and methodologies for creating evidence-based health guidelines. 13. Schünemann H, Brożek J, Guyatt G, and Oxman A authored the GRADE handbook, which provides a framework for grading the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations using the GRADE approach. 14. The Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions is a key resource for conducting systematic reviews and is available through the Cochrane organization. 15. Arbyn M, Simon M, Peeters E, Meijer CJLM, Berkhof J, Cuschieri K, and colleagues compiled a 2020 list of HPV assays suitable for primary cervical cancer screening. This was published in Clinical Microbiology and Infection in 2021, volume 27, issue 8, pages 1083–1095. 16. Canfell K, Kim JJ, Brisson M, Keane A, Simms KT, Caruana M, and others conducted a comparative modeling analysis on the mortality impact of achieving WHO cervical cancer elimination targets in 78 low-income and lower-middle-income countries. Their findings were published in The Lancet in 2020, volume 395, issue 10224, pages 591–603. 17. Brisson M, Kim JJ, Canfell K, Drolet M, Gingras G, Burger EA, and colleagues analyzed the impact of HPV vaccination and cervical screening on cervical cancer elimination in 78 low-income and lower-middle-income countries. This study was published in The Lancet in 2020, volume 395, issue 10224, pages 575–590. 18. Burger EA, Smith MA, Killen J, Sy S, Simms KT, Canfell K, and Kim JJ projected the time to cervical cancer elimination in the USA through a comparative modeling study. Their work appeared in The Lancet Public Health in 2020, volume 5, issue 4, pages e213–e222. 19. Hall MT, Simms KT, Lew JB, Smith MA, Brotherton JML, Saville M, and others modeled the projected timeframe for cervical cancer elimination in Australia. This study was published in The Lancet Public Health in 2018, volume 4, issue 1, pages e19–e27. 20. Kitchener HC, Canfell K, Gilham C, Sargent A, Roberts C, Desai M, and Peto J evaluated the clinical and cost-effectiveness of primary HPV cervical screening in England through extended follow-up of the ARTISTIC randomized trial cohort. Their findings were published in Health Technology Assessment in 2014, volume 18, issue 23, pages 1–196. 21. Lew J-B, Simms K, Smith M, Lewis H, Neal H, and Canfell K conducted effectiveness modeling and economic evaluation of primary HPV screening for cervical cancer prevention in New Zealand. This study was published in PLoS ONE in 2016, volume 11, issue 5, article e0151619. 22. Lew J-B, Simms KT, Smith MA, Hall M, Kang YJ, Xu XM, and others compared primary HPV testing versus cytology-based cervical screening in vaccinated and unvaccinated women in Australia. Their findings were published in The Lancet Public Health in 2017, volume 2, issue 2, pages e96–e107. 23. Shi JF, Canfell K, Lew JB, Zhao F-H, Legood R, Ning Y, and colleagues evaluated primary HPV-DNA testing in relation to visual inspection methods for cervical cancer screening in rural China. This epidemiologic and cost-effectiveness modeling study was published in BMC Cancer in 2011, volume 11, article 239. 24. Simms KT, Steinberg J, Caruana M, Smith MA, Lew J-B, Soerjomataram I, and others assessed the global impact of scaled-up HPV vaccination and cervical screening on cervical cancer elimination in 181 countries from 2020 to 2099. This modeling study was published in The Lancet Oncology in 2019, volume 20, pages 394–407.
